Tribes of India: Scheduled Tribes, regions and constitution

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

India's tribal communities, officially Scheduled Tribes and often called Adivasi, numbered about 8.6% of the population in the 2011 Census. They live across the country, with large populations in central India and the northeast. The Constitution protects them through the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, and the most vulnerable groups are listed as PVTGs.

We run guided visits to the Bhopal Tribal Museum and an oral history lab on respectful fieldwork for schools, colleges and adult groups.

Who are the Scheduled Tribes?

Scheduled Tribe is a legal and administrative category, not a description of a way of life. Under Article 342 of the Constitution, the President notifies which communities are Scheduled Tribes in each state or union territory, and Parliament can change the list by law. A community may be a Scheduled Tribe in one state and not in a neighbouring one.

Many communities prefer the word Adivasi, meaning original inhabitants, though not every community uses it, and in the northeast people usually name their own community instead. The communities are very diverse. They speak languages from the Austroasiatic, Tibeto-Burman, Dravidian and Indo-Aryan families, follow many different religious traditions, and earn their livelihoods through farming, forest work, herding, fishing, wage labour, trade, government service and the professions. Any single picture of a typical tribal life is misleading.

How many tribal people live in India?

According to the 2011 Census, Scheduled Tribes made up about 8.6% of India's population. The number of notified communities is large, and the same community can appear under different names in different states.

Most tribal people live in rural areas, but migration to towns and cities for education and work is growing. Figures from the next census will update this picture, so for current data check the Census of India and the Ministry of Tribal Affairs.

The Fifth and Sixth Schedules

The Constitution gives tribal areas special forms of governance through two schedules. They are the main reason that land and self-government feature so strongly in discussions of tribal rights.

FeatureFifth ScheduleSixth Schedule
Where it appliesScheduled Areas in states such as Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan and othersTribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram
Main institutionTribes Advisory Council in the stateAutonomous District Councils with law-making powers
Role of the GovernorCan modify or bar the application of laws in Scheduled AreasOversees the councils and certain matters of administration
Key protectionRestrictions on transfer of tribal landCouncils make laws on land, forests, customs and inheritance

Laws that shape tribal life today

Two later laws matter greatly. The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act of 1996, known as PESA, gives village assemblies in Fifth Schedule areas powers over local resources, minor forest produce and customary dispute resolution. The Forest Rights Act of 2006 recognises the rights of forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers to land they have cultivated and to community forest resources.

How these laws are implemented varies from state to state, and debates over mining, dams, conservation and displacement continue. The anthropologist's role in these debates is to record what communities themselves say about their land and history, rather than to speak over them.

Where tribal communities live: a regional view

Tribal communities are found in almost every state, but the pattern is uneven. Several northeastern states have a tribal majority, while central India has the largest number of tribal people in absolute terms. The groupings below are a broad guide, not a complete list.

  • Central India: Gond, Bhil, Baiga, Korku and Sahariya in Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra. The Gond and Bhil are among the largest tribal communities in the country.
  • Eastern India: Santal, Munda, Oraon and Ho in Jharkhand, Odisha and West Bengal; Kondh, Saora and Bonda in Odisha.
  • Western India: Bhil, Meena, Garasia and Warli in Rajasthan, Gujarat and Maharashtra.
  • Northeast India: Naga communities, Mizo, Khasi, Garo, Bodo, Karbi, Adi, Nyishi, Apatani and many more, each with its own language and institutions.
  • South India: Toda, Kota, Irula and Kurumba in the Nilgiris; Chenchu in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana; Soliga in Karnataka; Kani in Kerala.
  • Himalaya: Bhotia, Gaddi and Gujjar communities in the hills, and Ladakhi communities that are notified as Scheduled Tribes.
  • Islands: the Great Andamanese, Onge, Jarawa and Sentinelese in the Andamans, and the Shompen in the Nicobar Islands.

PVTGs: Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups

Within the Scheduled Tribes, the government identifies 75 communities as Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups. The criteria include a pre-agricultural level of technology, very low literacy, an economy at subsistence level and a stagnant or declining population. Examples include the Baiga of Madhya Pradesh, the Bonda of Odisha, the Cholanaikan of Kerala, the Toda of the Nilgiris, and the Onge, Jarawa and Sentinelese of the Andaman Islands.

The label is administrative and has been questioned by some scholars and community members, since it can describe people only by what they lack. It does, however, direct specific schemes and protections, especially for small island communities whose health is put at risk by outside contact.

Learning about tribal India with respect

The most useful starting point is to listen to how communities describe themselves and to read writers and scholars from those communities. Avoid treating tribal people as exotic, unchanging or living in the past: their histories are as long and as dynamic as anyone else's, and their art, music, knowledge of plants and folklore are living traditions.

Museums that work with tribal artists are a good way in. The Bhopal Tribal Museum was created with artists from communities across Madhya Pradesh, and a guided visit there shows homes, ritual life and art in the words of the communities. For longer study, read about ethnography and its ethics, and the broader guide to anthropology and tribal India. The oral history and neighbourhood memory lab teaches the consent-based interviewing that respectful study depends on.

Questions people ask

What percentage of India's population is tribal?

According to the 2011 Census, Scheduled Tribes made up about 8.6% of India's population. Updated figures will come from the next census. The share varies greatly by state: several northeastern states have tribal majorities, while some states have very small tribal populations.

Which is the largest tribe in India?

The Bhil and the Gond are usually named as the largest tribal communities in India, each with populations in the millions across several states of central and western India. The Santal of Jharkhand, West Bengal and Odisha are also among the largest.

What is the difference between the Fifth and Sixth Schedules?

The Fifth Schedule covers Scheduled Areas in many states and works through Tribes Advisory Councils and the Governor's special powers. The Sixth Schedule covers tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram and sets up Autonomous District Councils that can make laws on land, forests and customs.

How many PVTGs are there in India?

The government lists 75 Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups across India. They are identified by criteria such as pre-agricultural technology, low literacy, subsistence economy and stagnant or declining population. Examples include the Baiga, Bonda, Toda, Jarawa and Sentinelese.

Who decides which communities are Scheduled Tribes?

Under Article 342 of the Constitution, the President notifies the list of Scheduled Tribes for each state or union territory after consulting the Governor. After the first notification, only Parliament can add or remove communities by passing a law.
